cases.why: Iff is registered as a DEFINITION unfolding to And (p -> q) (q -> p), so a Lean biconditional lands on the conjunction and .mp/.mpr are its projections rather than methods of a fresh opaque proposition. Not an axiom and not an inductive: the trusted base is unchanged at 89.

The capability matches Lean exactly — the same two axioms, `reduceBool : Bool -> Bool` and `ofReduceBool : Pi(a b:Bool). reduceBool a = b -> a = b`, with identical types, and the whole bridge term kernel-checks in BOTH de Bruijn kernels. What differs is what stands behind them, and ours is the defensible side. Lean's `native_decide` trusts the Lean compiler, its C code generator, the emitted native object code, and the compiled form of the `Decidable` instance; none of that is re-run when someone independently re-checks the proof, so the artefact is believed rather than re-verified. LOGOS's `reduceBool` is discharged by `eval_bool`, a CBV evaluator living inside `logicaffeine_kernel` itself — which is exactly the crate a standalone re-check already trusts (the `examples/recheck` binary trusts this crate, `logicaffeine_base`, and a JSON parser, nothing else). Because `certificate::recheck` rebuilds the context from `StandardLibrary::register` and re-normalizes, an independent re-check RE-RUNS the evaluation instead of taking a compiled artefact's word for it; the test asserts exactly that. The trusted base for this feature is therefore smaller and auditable in one crate. The cost is real and is recorded rather than hidden: a proposition asserted by Lean's evaluator is not thereby asserted by ours, so a `native_decide` proof is not portable between the two systems on its own terms, and nothing in the certificate today distinguishes a theorem that used these two axioms from one that did not (that tracking gap is T06-017's work item, not a reason to call this case a gap).
